title: Area IV review: Preflight Lesson on a Maneuver to be Performed in Flight
intro: Area IV has one Task, the maneuver lesson, but the evaluator picks the maneuver from Areas VI through IX. So these questions put the Task to work on those maneuvers, with the evaluator playing your student: fitting a holding plan to a learner's stage, fixing an objective for a partial panel approach, describing a partial panel climb or a speed change in a turn, choosing an aid for holding entries, naming and correcting errors in steep turns and descents, and handling a demonstration that ATC changes in the middle.

questions.q: The evaluator picks holding (VII.B) and describes your learner: she has finished the IFH guide's partial panel and unusual attitude lessons but has never intercepted or tracked a course under the hood. Your library plan for holding covers all three entries, wind correction, DME legs and nonstandard turns in one session. How do you present it?
options: Unchanged: the Area IV NOTE lets you use library plans, so the evaluator expects the plan as written
Adapted: review course tracking first, then limit today's holding to what she can master
Faster: brief every item in less depth, since the AIH says too little material wastes a flight lesson
Refused: ask the evaluator for another maneuver, since holding does not fit her stage yet
questions.why: A flight lesson plan should fit the particular learner's background, flight experience and ability, and may need to be changed considerably [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. New material should be related to the previous lesson, and a person can master only a few principles or skills at a time: too much material results in confusion, too little only in inefficiency [[25:152|AIH 7-8]], so briefing everything faster is the wrong fix. The IFH lesson guide puts intercepting and tracking in the same lesson as holding, Lesson 8, right after unusual attitudes in Lesson 7 [[23:343|IFH B-2]], so tracking is the review this learner needs. The Area IV NOTE says library plans may be used, not that they must be presented unchanged, and the NOTE has the evaluator, not the applicant, select the maneuver [[FAA-S-8081-9E:30|PTS Area IV NOTE]].

questions.q: The evaluator picks the approach with loss of primary flight instrument indicators (IX.B). Your objective reads: "Fly the VOR approach to the MDA, holding the course within half scale and each altitude within 100 feet." The evaluator, playing a student who trains in both a six-pack trainer and a glass-panel trainer, asks: "But what if I'm in the glass airplane? What fails?" Which part of the objective needs work?
options: The behavior: reword it as "gain an awareness of" partial panel approaches
The criteria: tighter limits settle which instruments the student will use
The conditions: name the airplane and which instruments are covered or failed
Nothing: a student's "what if" belongs in the development, not the objective
questions.why: Conditions explain the rules for showing the skill, such as equipment and limiting parameters, and when a reader of the objective asks "But, what if ...?", the conditions are confusing and need clarification [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Here they must say which instruments are lost: in an analog airplane, partial panel means the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; on an electronic flight display, the AHRS simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. The criteria are already measurable, which is their job [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]; tightening them does not answer the question. "Awareness of" cannot be measured very well and should be avoided [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

questions.q: The evaluator picks constant airspeed climbs and descents (VI.D) and asks you to include partial panel. Which climb entry do you describe as the one the IFH finds easier to control on partial panel?
options: From cruise: raise the nose and add climb power together, letting the speed bleed off in the climb
From climb speed: slow to it in level flight first, then raise the nose as power comes up
From cruise: add climb power first, then let the airplane climb on its own until the VSI settles
From climb speed: set the target rate on the VSI first, then use power to correct the airspeed
questions.why: The IFH says climb entries on partial panel are more easily and accurately controlled if the maneuver is entered from climbing speed: first complete the reduction from cruise to climb speed in straight-and-level flight, then raise the pitch attitude as power goes to the climb setting [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The entry from cruise, with power added during or after the pitch change, is also in the IFH, but it is the one the IFH finds harder to control on partial panel [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The IFH's descent entry works the same way, slowing to the descent speed in level flight first, and is effective with or without an attitude indicator [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The VSI becomes primary for pitch in a constant rate climb, once the vertical speed nears the desired value [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; in a constant airspeed climb the ASI is primary for pitch once the airplane stabilizes [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Brief the common error with it: overcontrolling pitch on the climb entry [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

questions.q: The evaluator picks steep turns (VI.G). Playing your student, he loses altitude on every entry: his back pressure always comes late, and the bank keeps steepening while the altimeter unwinds. How do you describe your analysis and correction of this error?
options: Have him hold the bank and pull harder, since more back pressure always brings the nose back up
Have him add full power before each entry, since the lost vertical lift is purely a power problem
Have him repeat the full steep turn until the timing comes, since repetition fixes a late pitch input
Have him roll out and analyze it, then build up from shallower turns as his cross-check speeds up
questions.why: If pitch control is consistently late on steep turn entries, the IFH says to roll out immediately to straight-and-level flight and analyze possible errors, practice shallower turns first to learn the attitude changes and control responses, then increase the bank as a quicker cross-check and control technique develop [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. That matches the AIH's simple-to-complex strategy, which lets a learner gain confidence on the simplest skill first [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Overbanking without adjusting pitch reaches a point where more back pressure only tightens the turn without raising the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Pitch control is usually the hardest part of the maneuver because of the reduced vertical lift [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and the PTS lists failure to recognize and correct pitch, bank or power errors as a steep turn common error [[FAA-S-8081-9E:36|PTS VI.G K2a]].

questions.q: After rolling out of a steep turn, the evaluator, as your student, holds the miniature airplane level on the attitude indicator with the ball centered, but the heading indicator keeps creeping. He asks why he cannot hold a heading. Which error do you name, and what do you tell him?
options: Precession of the horizon bar: the airplane is still turning, so stop the heading change and retrim
A slipping turn: the ball is wrong, so hold rudder until the heading indicator stops moving
A failed heading indicator: cover it and finish on the compass, then write it up afterward
Fixation: leave the heading indicator out of the cross-check for 20 seconds until it settles
questions.why: The IFH lists failure to check for precession of the horizon bar after recovery from a turn: if the heading indicator shows a heading change while the attitude indicator shows level flight, the airplane is turning; with the ball centered the attitude gyro has precessed, while an off-center ball points to a slipping or skidding turn. The fix is to center the ball, check the attitude and heading indicators, stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Leaving the heading indicator out for about 20 seconds applies during an established standard rate turn, before the lead point, not after the roll-out [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. The PTS lists failure to compensate for precession of the horizon bar as a steep turn common error [[FAA-S-8081-9E:36|PTS VI.G K2b]].

questions.q: Briefing holding entries (VII.B), you have spent three minutes describing the entry sectors in words, and your student looks lost. What do the AIH guidelines for instructional aids suggest?
options: Keep talking: the AIH calls aids a crutch, so a skilled instructor does without them
Sketch the pattern and its entry sectors on the marker board, and let her draw too
Hand her a busy poster with every holding rule on it, so nothing is left out
Save entries for the airplane, where the moving needle shows her the sector
questions.why: Aids are often appropriate when a point is complex and difficult to put into words, when instructors find themselves forming visual images, or when learners are puzzled by an explanation [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. Relatively simple aids are generally best [[25:126|AIH 5-23]], words on an aid should be kept to a minimum, and the AIH's warning is against using aids as a crutch, not against using them [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. The marker board is an excellent medium for joint learner-instructor activity [[25:128|AIH 5-25]], and the IFH draws the parallel, teardrop and direct entries as sectors around the fix in Figure 10-6 [[23:303|IFH 10-12]]. The explanation phase is done before the flight lesson [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

questions.q: The evaluator picks change of airspeed in turning flight (VI.C). In your description, what happens to the bank as the airspeed comes down in a standard rate turn, and which of the two IFH methods do you teach first?
options: Hold the bank; start the speed change together with the turn entry
More bank; start the speed change once the turn is established
Less bank, higher nose; start the speed change once the turn is established
Less bank and a lower nose; start the speed change together with the turn entry
questions.why: The bank angle needed for a given rate of turn is proportional to the true airspeed, so as the airspeed is reduced in a standard rate turn, decrease the bank and increase the pitch attitude to hold altitude [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Of the two methods, changing the airspeed after the turn is established is easier than starting it with the turn entry [[23:185|IFH 7-24]], which fits the AIH's simple-to-complex strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. With either method, the rate of cross-check must increase as power is reduced [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

questions.q: Playing your student in constant airspeed descents (VI.D), the evaluator levels off at cruise speed from a 500 fpm descent. He adds cruise power at the lead point, the nose comes up, and the airplane rises 80 feet above the target altitude. How do you name the error and the fix?
options: Ballooning: hold forward pressure as the power comes up, keeping the descent rate until about 50 feet above
Too little lead: start this level-off at 10 percent of the vertical speed, the same lead as from a climb
Chasing the VSI: cover it and level off by the altimeter alone on the next try, to stop the overshoot
Too much lead: wait until the altimeter reaches the altitude, then add power and level off together
questions.why: The IFH names ballooning on level-offs from descents: the nose pitches up because the pilot fails to hold the descending attitude with forward pressure as power goes to the cruise setting [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. From 500 fpm to a speed above the descent speed, lead by 100-150 feet, add cruise power at the lead point, hold forward pressure to keep the descent rate until about 50 feet above the altitude, then set the level attitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The 10 percent lead is the IFH figure for climbs [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], and too little lead makes the airplane overshoot the altitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], which in a descent means going below it; waiting until the altimeter reaches the altitude ignores that 100-150 foot lead. Chasing the vertical speed comes from failing to cross-check the VSI against the other pitch instruments [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

questions.q: The evaluator picks DME arcs (VII.A). Your library plan was written around a DME receiver, but the airplane you are briefing for has an IFR-certified GPS and no DME. What do you do with the plan?
options: Keep it as written: the evaluator grades the plan, not how it fits the airplane
Fly the arc by timing, since a clock can stand in for the DME on any arc
Drop the arc: the PTS lets arcs be taught only in a DME-equipped airplane
Revise it for this airplane: IFR GPS may be used in place of DME on an arc
questions.why: Each lesson should be planned for the conditions under which the training is conducted, and the aids available have a great influence on the plan [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]; a plan is revised as aids become available or unavailable [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The IFH says IFR-certified GPS equipment may be substituted for DME when flying a DME arc [[23:301|IFH 10-10]]. The PTS does not limit arcs to DME-equipped airplanes: its Area VII NOTE has arcs tested orally when the airplane lacks DME [[FAA-S-8081-9E:38|PTS Area VII NOTE]], and its VII.A NOTE allows arcs that are charted and available, including RNAV substitution [[FAA-S-8081-9E:38|PTS VII.A NOTE]]. No source here describes flying an arc by timing alone.

questions.q: The evaluator picks loss of communications (IX.A) and describes a learner two lessons from her checkride who flies the procedures well. Which kind of objective does the AIH point you to for her lost-communications lesson?
options: Performance-based only, since decision-based objectives suit early learners still building skills
An awareness objective, since judgment cannot be measured and so can have no stated criteria
None stated, since at her stage the AIH has learners set their own goals once the lesson starts
Decision-based: in a scenario, she picks route, altitude and when to leave the clearance limit
questions.why: As the learner progresses through higher levels of performance and understanding, the AIH says to shift the training focus to decision-based objectives, which suit scenario-based training [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] and teach the learner to gather information and make informed, safe and timely decisions through dynamic, meaningful scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. For lost communications, the IFH says the pilot must know at any point what route to fly, what altitude to fly and when to continue beyond a clearance limit [[23:333|IFH 11-8]], which makes good decision points. Clearly defined objectives that the learner understands are essential, and phrases like "awareness of" cannot be measured very well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

questions.q: You briefed the published missed approach (VIII.C) and are now demonstrating it. At the missed approach point, ATC specifies an alternate missed approach with a different heading and altitude. What do you do?
options: Fly the published procedure you briefed, since a demonstration must match its explanation
Fly ATC's procedure and keep quiet until the postflight, so the demonstration stays clean
Fly ATC's procedure and say at once why the demonstration now differs from your brief
Stop the demonstration, land, and repeat the whole brief on the ground before trying again
questions.why: At the missed approach point, the pilot must comply with the missed approach instructions for the procedure being used or with an alternate missed approach procedure specified by ATC [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21]]. The AIH says that if, due to unanticipated circumstances, the demonstration does not closely conform to the explanation, the deviation should be immediately acknowledged and explained [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], so waiting for the postflight is the tempting but wrong choice. Learners generally imitate the instructor's performance [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Application: an ATC change in mid-demonstration is a ready-made lesson in flying the clearance actually issued.

questions.q: Your library plan for the partial panel nonprecision approach (VIII.A) sets today's completion standard at "Explain" in learner-centered grading. What will the learner be able to do at the end of the lesson?
options: Describe the approach and the concepts behind it, but still need help to fly it
Fly the approach to the MDA without help, finding and fixing her own errors
Plan and fly the approach, with your coaching correcting the errors you point out
Name the steps of the approach, but not yet the reasons behind them or how to fly it
questions.why: Explain means the learner can describe the scenario activity and understand the underlying concepts, principles and procedures, but needs assistance to execute the maneuver. Describe lacks that understanding of the underlying concepts, Practice means she plans and executes it with coaching correcting the errors you identify, and Perform means she does it without instructor assistance [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Listing the criteria of the objectives sets the plan's completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], and they should gradually reach or exceed the ACS/PTS before checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. The Area VIII NOTE requires at least one nonprecision approach without the gyroscopic heading and attitude indicators [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]].
